With 13 years in procurement – including 8+ years leading IT tenders and hardware sourcing – I've developed a deep conviction: the future of purchasing is automated, intelligent, and human-centred. I believe in optimism, openness, and the power of connecting the right people.

header.title: GardenPin
header.lead: A weekend build — from a Moleskine sketch to a working garden-planning app with companion-planting recommendations, offline mode, and a hand-rolled canvas grid.

problem.title: Problem
problem.body: Every spring I sketch a layout for my three raised beds in a notebook, lose it by July, and rebuild from memory the following year. Companion-planting matters — basil and tomatoes thrive together, basil and rue do not — but the rules live in a dozen scattered articles. There was no single tool that let me draw a bed, place plants, and see which neighbours would help or hurt.

solution.title: Solution
solution.body: A phone-friendly, offline-first web app where each raised bed is a top-down grid. Plants are dragged onto tiles; a companion-planting graph scores their neighbours in real-time. Sowing dates trigger watering and harvest reminders via the browser's Notification API. No accounts, no servers, no tracking — just a 32-character device ID in a cookie and an opt-in sync endpoint.

items.title: Companion-planting graph
items.body: 278-plant catalogue with companion / antagonist edges encoded as a sparse adjacency table. Drag-and-drop scoring picks tiles where neighbours boost growth and avoid known antagonists.

items.title: Interactive map + canvas grid
items.body: ~140 lines of vanilla canvas: pan via pointer events, pinch-zoom around the cursor, plants render as coloured circles + emoji. No charting library, no map tiles, no SVG.

items.title: iCal export to iOS calendar
items.body: Sowing, watering and harvest tasks ship as a one-tap subscribable .ics feed. Add it once on your iPhone and reminders appear next to the rest of your calendar — no extra app to open.

items.title: Offline-first by default
items.body: All user data lives in localStorage. A 32-character device ID lets you opt in to single-endpoint sync. No accounts, no passwords, no third-party trackers.

items.what: Started with React Native + Mapbox. Three hours later: simulator certs unresolved, Mapbox demanding a credit card. Scrap.
Reset. Plain Next.js 14 + canvas. Drew the first bed grid in 40 minutes.
Curated the 84-plant catalogue and the companion / antagonist relations. Detour through r/permaculture for weighting.
Drag-and-drop pin placement, neighbour scoring, score visualisation on hover.
Reminder generation from sowing dates. Web Notifications API wired up. First end-to-end run.
Polish: dark mode, keyboard navigation, exporting beds as PNG, deploy to Vercel. Ship.

screenshots.title: Screenshots
screenshots.caption: Screenshot coming with v1.1 release
items: Bed editor — drag plants onto the grid

items.title: Friction is the enemy of weekend builds
items.body: The right stack is the one you can reach without burning a half-day on certs, billing accounts, or framework debates. I dropped React Native the second it cost me three hours.

items.title: Canvas beats charting libraries when the geometry is yours
items.body: I almost installed Konva. The whole map ended up in 140 lines of vanilla canvas, and I understand every pixel. Reach for a library when you'd be re-implementing it badly — not before.

items.title: Curate data before you build the visualisation
items.body: I started with the canvas and discovered halfway through Saturday that my plant data was incomplete. A weekend build doesn't have time for two passes — get the data right first, then make it pretty.

items.title: Skip backend cron jobs when client-side derivations work
items.body: Reminders are deterministic functions of your plant data. I generate them in the browser and use the Notification API — no worker, no queue, no infrastructure. Hobby apps reward this kind of simplification.

header.badge: Case Study · Side Project · Health Tech
header.title: Health Analyzer
header.lead: An offline AI health tracker. Upload a lab report, an OCR pipeline pulls every marker out of the PDF, and a locally-running Llama 3.1 explains — in plain language — what sits outside the reference range. Nothing leaves the laptop.

problem.title: Problem
problem.body: Twice a year I get a stack of lab results — twelve PDFs, fifty markers, three different reference-range conventions. The interesting story is rarely a single bad value; it's the trend across two years. But I'm not about to paste my full blood panel into ChatGPT, and the SaaS trackers that promise this either charge €15/month or quietly forward your data to a third-party API.

why_local.title: Why local Ollama
why_local.body: Health data is the textbook case for staying on-device. Hormone panels, lipid trends, anything liver-related — once it leaves your machine, you don't get it back. Running Llama 3.1 8B through Ollama means the model loads in 4 GB of RAM, runs at ~30 tokens/s on an M2 Air, and the only network traffic the app makes is checking for Ollama on localhost:11434. No accounts, no API keys, no cloud bill that scales with how curious I am that week.

how_it_works.title: How it works — OCR + bulk import
how_it_works.body: Drop a folder of PDFs onto the import zone. Tesseract OCR scans each page, a small parser detects the marker name + value + unit + reference range (Czech and German labs use different layouts, so there's a per-lab template registry). Markers get normalised, deduplicated against history, and stored in Postgres. Once a year's worth is in, you click "Explain" — the app builds a structured markdown summary (current value vs. range vs. 12-month trend) and ships that, not the raw PDFs, to the local LLM. The model returns three sections: what to watch, what to ignore, what to ask the GP.

items.title: 100% local inference
items.body: Llama 3.1 8B via Ollama on localhost. No API keys, no rate limits, no subscription. Works on a plane.

items.title: Bulk PDF import + OCR
items.body: Drag a folder of lab PDFs onto the import zone. Tesseract pulls text, a per-lab parser extracts marker name + value + unit + range.

items.title: Trend analysis across years
items.body: Each marker is normalised and stored over time, so you see whether ferritin is genuinely drifting or just noisy week-to-week.

items.title: Plain-language explanations
items.body: The LLM gets a structured summary, not the raw PDFs. It returns three sections: what to watch, what to ignore, what to ask the GP.

items.what: Painful spike: paste one lab PDF into Claude and ask for analysis. The output was great. The €0.40 per request was not the issue — sending the panel to a third party was.
Installed Ollama, pulled llama3.1:8b, wired up a tiny Next.js page that POSTs to localhost:11434. First local response in 6 seconds.
OCR pipeline with Tesseract. First three Czech lab templates parsed cleanly; the German one needed a per-lab regex.
Postgres schema for markers + history. Bulk import of 18 months of PDFs. First trend view.
Prompt engineering: structured markdown summary, few-shot examples for tone, three-section output. Quality jumped past the original cloud version.
Adding lab templates as I encounter new layouts. Next: an Ollama-based natural-language query layer ("show me ferritin since 2023").

screenshots.title: Screenshots
screenshots.caption: Screenshots redacted — real lab data inside
items: Bulk import — drop a folder of PDFs

items.title: Local-first changes what you let yourself store
items.body: When inference costs €0 and data never leaves the laptop, you stop self-censoring what you import. The dataset got richer because the privacy cost dropped to zero.

items.title: Prompt > parameter count, again
items.body: Llama 3.1 8B with a structured summary beats GPT-4 with raw PDFs. The win was in the input shape, not the model size — same lesson I keep relearning.

items.title: OCR is the unsexy 80%
items.body: I budgeted a weekend for the LLM and an evening for OCR. It was the other way around. Lab PDFs have wildly inconsistent layouts; a per-lab template registry was unavoidable.

items.title: Health data deserves a higher bar than 'we encrypt in transit'
items.body: Most SaaS trackers will happily process your blood panel through a third-party LLM. I'm not willing to assume that ends well. Local-first wasn't a feature — it was the whole reason to build it.
